units.title: Countable and uncountable nouns; determiners
notes: Countable nouns have a plural: one ticket, three tickets. Some plurals are irregular: man, men; child, children; foot, feet.
Uncountable nouns (money, advice, information, furniture, news) have no plural and take a singular verb: The furniture is new.
To count them, use a phrase: a piece of advice, two bottles of water.
many, a few, several + plural nouns; much, a little + uncountable nouns; some, any, no, a lot of, plenty of with both.

items.q: How ___ did you spend on online shopping last month?
items.why: money is uncountable, so How much

items.q: Can you give me some ___ about refunds?
items.why: information is uncountable and has no plural

items.q: There aren't ___ promotions in this shop at the moment.
The furniture in that shop ___ very expensive.
items.why: furniture is uncountable, so singular verb

items.q: I only made ___ purchases this month, so I saved money.
We have ___ of time to exchange the shoes. The shop closes at nine.
She gave me two useful ___ of advice about buying online.
There is ___ money left on my card, so I can't buy it.
items.why: positive verb + no means not any

items.q: I tried on ___ jackets before I found the right one.
All the ___ (child) in the queue were waiting to see the new toys.
How ___ (much / many) receipts have you kept?
The news about the discount ___ (be) great. I'm going to the shop right now!
items.why: news is uncountable, so singular verb

items.q: The shop assistant served three ___ (woman) before me.
I haven't got ___ (much / many) luggage, so I can walk to the hotel.
Could I have ___ (a / some) bread with my soup, please?
items.why: bread is uncountable, so no a

items.q: The shop gave me a good advice about refunds.
a: The shop gave me good advice about refunds.
The shop gave me some good advice about refunds.
The shop gave me a good piece of advice about refunds.
items.why: advice is uncountable, so no a

items.q: How much charges are there for delivery?
a: How many charges are there for delivery?

items.q: My new trousers is too small, so I will send them back.
a: My new trousers are too small, so I will send them back.

items.q: much / spend / how / on clothes / you / money / do
a: How much money do you spend on clothes?

items.q: any / there / in the sale / weren't / shoes / nice
a: There weren't any nice shoes in the sale.

units.title: -ing forms
notes: Spelling: read, reading; make, making; swim, swimming.
Use -ing after verbs of liking and disliking: enjoy, love, like, hate, dislike, don't mind, can't stand. I can't stand waiting.
Use -ing after a preposition: good at, bad at, keen on, interested in, afraid of, tired of. Marta is keen on skating.
Use -ing as the subject of a sentence: Learning a language takes time.

items.q: My sociable cousin loves ___ new people.
He is very talented. He's really good ___ drawing.
___ with unreliable people is really annoying.
I don't mind ___ for you. I'm not in a hurry.
She's afraid ___ speaking in public because she's anxious.
Are you interested ___ joining the drama club?
My brother can't stand ___ with silly people.
I'm tired of ___ to your unkind jokes.
We are keen ___ trying the new climbing wall.
My loyal friend enjoys ___ (help) other people.
___ (swim) in the sea is my favourite summer activity.
items.why: -ing as subject, and double the m

items.q: She's bad at ___ (make) decisions because she's too anxious.
items.why: bad at + -ing, and make loses the -e

items.q: I hate ___ (sit) next to people who disagree with everything.
He's a sensible boy and he dislikes ___ (argue) with his parents.
Thank you for ___ (be) so thoughtful when I was ill.
I enjoy to spend time with easygoing people.
a: I enjoy spending time with easygoing people.

items.q: She is interested in learn about other cultures.
a: She is interested in learning about other cultures.

items.q: Run every morning is good for you.
a: Running every morning is good for you.
items.why: use -ing when a verb is the subject

items.q: at / my sister / very good / is / remembering / birthdays
a: My sister is very good at remembering birthdays.

items.q: can't / I / for / waiting / stand / unreliable / people
a: I can't stand waiting for unreliable people.

units.title: Present simple and present continuous
notes: Present simple for habits, routines and facts: The shop opens at nine. Add -s or -es for he, she, it. Use do, does, don't, doesn't.
Present continuous (am, is, are + -ing) for actions happening now or around now: Be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
Present continuous also for fixed future arrangements: We are playing in the final next Saturday.
State verbs (want, know, believe, understand, belong) are not normally used in the continuous.

items.q: My sister ___ a tennis tournament every summer.
items.why: every summer is a routine, and she takes -s

items.q: Listen! The spectators ___ because someone has scored a goal.
items.why: Listen! shows it is happening now

items.q: ___ your team usually beat the other schools?
items.why: your team is it, so Does

items.q: I ___ to join the sailing club this year.
items.why: want is a state verb, so no continuous

items.q: He ___ like losing matches. He gets really angry.
What ___ the swimmers doing at the moment?
items.why: the swimmers is they, so are

items.q: This term we ___ for a big competition, so we practise every day.
items.why: this term is a temporary period around now

items.q: The winner always ___ a gold medal.
We ___ in the final next Saturday. It's all arranged.
Right now the climbers ___ (rest) at the top of the mountain.
items.why: right now needs the present continuous

items.q: My cousin ___ (not belong) to any sports club.
items.why: belong is a state verb: present simple

items.q: How often ___ (your dad go) surfing?
items.why: How often asks about a habit: does + subject + infinitive

items.q: Be quiet, please. I ___ (watch) the final and it's very exciting.
A good competitor never ___ (miss) an opportunity to practise.
She ___ (not run) this week because she has hurt her foot.
My brother play football for the school team.
a: My brother plays football for the school team.

items.q: I am not believing that we won the match!
a: I don't believe that we won the match!
I do not believe that we won the match!

items.q: Do your sister have a go at new sports?
a: Does your sister have a go at new sports?
items.why: your sister is she, so Does

items.q: having / the canoeists / a rest / now / why / are
a: Why are the canoeists having a rest now?

items.q: never / gives / our coach / to play / me / the chance
a: Our coach never gives me the chance to play.
items.why: never goes before the main verb

units.title: Past simple and used to
notes: Past simple for finished actions, often with a time: We moved here in 2019. Regular verbs add -ed; many verbs are irregular (blow, blew; rise, rose; shake, shook).
Negatives and questions use didn't or did + infinitive: I didn't see him. Did you call her? The verb be uses was or were.
used to + infinitive for past habits and states that are not true now: I used to be scared of storms.
Negative and question: didn't use to, Did you use to ...? (no d after did).

items.q: The tornado ___ away the roof of our garage last year.
___ the firefighters put out the fire quickly?
We ___ to have snowstorms every winter, but now it rarely snows.
My town didn't ___ to have floods.
items.why: after didn't write use, not used

items.q: The river ___ two metres after the storm last week.
Did you ___ to be afraid of lightning when you were little?
items.why: after Did write use, not used

items.q: The ground ___ for a minute during the earthquake.
It ___ rain much last summer, so the river was low.
Where ___ you when the storm started?
items.why: the verb be with you in the past is were

items.q: Several trees ___ (fall) down in the storm last night.
The old factory ___ (burn) down in 2015.
We ___ (not go) out yesterday because it was pouring with rain.
When I was a child, I ___ (use to) love playing in the snow. Now I hate the cold.
items.why: a past state that is not true now

items.q: ___ (you see) the lightning last night? It was amazing!
items.why: last night needs Did + subject + infinitive

items.q: The sun ___ (come) out after the storm, and then we cleared up the garden.
Did the flood destroyed many houses?
a: Did the flood destroy many houses?

items.q: I use to live near a river when I was young.
a: I used to live near a river when I was young.

items.q: There was a lot of floods in this area last century.
a: There were a lot of floods in this area last century.

items.q: to / in / used / a lot / it / April / rain
a: It used to rain a lot in April.
In April it used to rain a lot.

items.q: didn't / the / the earthquake / down / fall / during / school
a: The school didn't fall down during the earthquake.
During the earthquake, the school didn't fall down.

units.title: Past simple and past continuous
notes: Past continuous is was or were + -ing: I was reading. They weren't listening. Was she sleeping?
Use it for an action in progress at a moment in the past, or the background of a story: The sun was shining.
Past simple for a short action that interrupts it: I was sewing when I cut my finger.
when + past simple; while + past continuous. State verbs (know, want) stay in the past simple.

items.q: I was sewing a button on my shirt when I ___ my finger.
items.why: the short action is past simple, and cut is irregular

items.q: While Dad ___ the bike, I made some sandwiches.
items.why: the longer action after while is past continuous

items.q: What ___ you making when I phoned you?
The sun was shining and the birds ___ when we set off.
When the chair broke, my grandad ___ it with some glue.
items.why: one action after another: past simple

items.q: I saw a great idea for recycling bottles ___ I was looking online.
They ___ listening when the teacher explained how to design the poster.
___ she decorating the cake when you arrived?
We were rebuilding the wall when it ___ to rain.
items.why: the short action after when is past simple

items.q: At ten o'clock last night I ___ (design) a logo for our band.
items.why: in progress at a moment in the past

items.q: He ___ (drop) the vase while he was decorating it.
items.why: short action: past simple, double the p

items.q: While we ___ (create) our website, the computer crashed.
My mum ___ (not work) when I got home. She was reading in the garden.
items.why: in progress at that moment: wasn't + -ing

items.q: When I ___ (open) the box, I found an old sewing machine.
What ___ (you do) at six o'clock yesterday evening? I called you three times.
items.why: question about an action in progress

items.q: I was knowing how to sew when I was seven.
a: I knew how to sew when I was seven.
items.why: know is a state verb, so past simple

items.q: We were paint the bedroom when Grandma arrived.
a: We were painting the bedroom when Grandma arrived.

items.q: I was customising my trainers when my sister was coming in.
a: I was customising my trainers when my sister came in.
items.why: the short action after when is past simple

items.q: was / the bike / when / he / mending / I / arrived
a: He was mending the bike when I arrived.
When I arrived, he was mending the bike.
I was mending the bike when he arrived.
When he arrived, I was mending the bike.
items.why: continuous for the long action, simple after when

items.q: her finger / she / while / was sewing / she / hurt
a: She hurt her finger while she was sewing.
While she was sewing, she hurt her finger.

units.title: Modals of obligation, necessity and advice: must, have to, should, ought to
notes: must, should and ought to never change form and are followed by the infinitive: You must stop. He should rest. We ought to leave.
have to changes like a normal verb: she has to, Do you have to?, he doesn't have to, we had to.
mustn't means it is not allowed. don't have to means it is not necessary.
should, shouldn't and ought to give advice: You ought to see a doctor.

items.q: You ___ touch that pan. You'll burn yourself!
items.why: it is dangerous, so do not do it

items.q: You ___ to see a doctor about that cough.
items.why: only ought is followed by to

items.q: It's a holiday tomorrow, so we ___ get up early.
My dad ___ wear glasses when he drives.
If your leg aches, you ___ rest it.
___ she have to stay in hospital tonight?
items.why: question with she: Does ... have to

items.q: You ___ blow your nose so loudly in class. It's rude.
He must ___ in bed until he recovers.
You ___ pay to see the school nurse. It's free.
items.why: free means it is not necessary to pay

items.q: Yesterday I cut my hand, so I ___ (have to) go to hospital.
items.why: the past of have to and must is had to

items.q: My sister ___ (not have to) take any medicine now. She has recovered.
___ (we have to) breathe through a mask in the laboratory, or can we choose?
items.why: questions with have to use do

items.q: You're yawning a lot. You ___ (should / mustn't) go to bed earlier.
Your nose is bleeding. You ___ (ought / should) to sit down.
Visitors ___ (mustn't / don't have to) smoke in the hospital. It's forbidden.
You should to drink more water.
He musts stay at home today.
a: He must stay at home today.

items.q: She don't have to come to the hospital with me.
a: She doesn't have to come to the hospital with me.
She does not have to come to the hospital with me.

items.q: to / when / ought / you / you / cough / cover your mouth
a: You ought to cover your mouth when you cough.
When you cough, you ought to cover your mouth.

items.q: have / wear / in / do / a helmet / we / to / the gym
a: Do we have to wear a helmet in the gym?

units.title: Present perfect and past simple
notes: Present perfect is have or has + past participle: I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten?
Past simple for finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago): I lost my keys on Monday.
Present perfect when the time is not said or the result matters now: I've lost my keys.
ever, never, just, already, yet, so far, since and for are common with the present perfect.

items.q: I ___ my favourite band live in 2023.
Have you ___ been to a music festival?
The DJ hasn't arrived ___. Everyone is waiting.
items.why: yet goes at the end of a negative

items.q: She ___ three albums so far.
items.why: so far means up to now

items.q: When ___ the concert start last night?
items.why: last night is a finished time

items.q: We've ___ bought tickets for the gig, so we don't need to queue.
He ___ the guitar since he was six.
The band ___ their first song ten years ago.
I've ___ heard their new single. It was on the radio a minute ago.
items.why: just means a very short time ago

items.q: My cousin ___ (perform) at a big festival last August.
items.why: last August is a finished time

items.q: I ___ (never meet) a celebrity in my life.
___ (you watch) the music video yet? It came out this morning.
The guitarist ___ (leave) the band in 2021 and started a solo career.
Oh no! I ___ (forget) the lyrics, and I'm on stage in two minutes!
She ___ (not achieve) her dream yet, but she is still trying.
I have been to a great gig last weekend.
a: I went to a great gig last weekend.
items.why: last weekend needs the past simple

items.q: Did you ever played in a band?
a: Have you ever played in a band?

items.q: She has wrote all the lyrics herself.
a: She has written all the lyrics herself.
items.why: the participle of write is written

items.q: has / the band / their new album / advertised / already
a: The band has already advertised their new album.
The band has advertised their new album already.
items.why: already goes between has and the participle

items.q: ever / to a concert hall / you / been / have
a: Have you ever been to a concert hall?

units.title: Comparative and superlative adjectives
notes: Short adjectives add -er and -est: tall, taller, the tallest. Spelling: large, larger; hot, hotter; easy, easier.
Longer adjectives use more and the most: more expensive, the most expensive. less is the opposite of more.
Irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst; far, further, the furthest.
Use than after comparatives and as + adjective + as to say things are equal: It isn't as new as yours.

items.q: This cosy café is ___ than the one in the square.
It's the ___ building in the city. It was built in Roman times.
Our new flat isn't as modern ___ yours.
The second hotel was even ___ than the first. It was terrible!
That was ___ spectacular show I have ever seen.
The train is ___ expensive than the plane, so let's go by train.
My bedroom is the ___ room in the house in winter.
Who lives ___ from the school, you or Sam?
Traditional markets are ___ than supermarkets in my opinion.
Today the bread is ___ (fresh) than it was yesterday.
That's the ___ (unusual) house in our street. It looks like a boat!
My old phone was ___ (good) than this brand new one. I want it back!
July was the ___ (dry) month of last year.
This sofa is ___ (comfortable) than that classic chair.
It was the ___ (bad) storm in the town's history.
This museum is more big than the old one.
a: This museum is bigger than the old one.
items.why: short adjectives take -er, and double the g

items.q: It is the most cheap hotel in the town.
a: It is the cheapest hotel in the town.

items.q: Madrid is not as old than Rome.
a: Madrid is not as old as Rome.

items.q: in / the / restaurant / is / this / the town / oldest
a: This is the oldest restaurant in the town.
This restaurant is the oldest in the town.

items.q: than / is / much more / the new stadium / modern / the old one
a: The new stadium is much more modern than the old one.
The old one is much more modern than the new stadium.

units.title: Future forms: present continuous, will, be going to and future continuous
notes: Present continuous + a time for fixed arrangements: I'm seeing the dentist at four.
will + infinitive for predictions, offers and promises: I think robots will do more jobs. I'll carry that for you.
be going to + infinitive for plans and intentions: We're going to paint my room this weekend.
Future continuous (will or won't be + -ing) for an action in progress at a future time: This time tomorrow I'll be travelling.

items.q: This time tomorrow we ___ the satellite launch on TV.
items.why: in progress at a future time: will be + -ing

items.q: Your phone has no power. Give it to me, I ___ it in for you.
I ___ the engineer at three o'clock. It's in my diary.
I think electric cars ___ much cheaper in ten years.
She's going ___ her invention to the science fair. She has planned it for weeks.
___ you be using the charger this evening?
items.why: future continuous question: Will + subject + be + -ing

items.q: Don't phone me at nine. I ___ an experiment then.
items.why: an action in progress at nine

items.q: I promise I ___ your tablet again without asking.
In 2050 most people ___ be using petrol as fuel.
At ten o'clock tomorrow morning I ___ (sit) in my science exam.
items.why: in progress at a future time

items.q: We've bought all the parts. We ___ (build) a robot this weekend.
'The display is too dark.' 'Wait, I ___ (fix) it for you now.'
items.why: an offer at the moment of speaking

items.q: This time next year my brother ___ (study) engineering at university.
items.why: this time next year: will be + -ing

items.q: The technician ___ (come) at four this afternoon. Mum arranged it yesterday.
I'm sure this connection ___ (not work) during the storm tonight.
Will you be use the computer tonight?
a: Will you be using the computer tonight?

items.q: They going to test the invention tomorrow.
a: They are going to test the invention tomorrow.
They're going to test the invention tomorrow.

items.q: I think it will rains tomorrow.
a: I think it will rain tomorrow.

items.q: be / at midnight / will / I / sleeping
a: I will be sleeping at midnight.
At midnight I will be sleeping.

items.q: to / are / the old satellite / going / they / replace / next year
a: They are going to replace the old satellite next year.
Next year they are going to replace the old satellite.

units.title: Zero, first and second conditionals
notes: Zero: if + present, present. For things that are always true: If you heat ice, it melts.
First: if + present, will or won't + infinitive. For real future possibilities: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
Second: if + past simple, would or wouldn't + infinitive. For unreal or unlikely situations: If I had a boat, I would sail to Ibiza.
No will or would in the if-clause. unless means if not.

items.q: If you heat metal, it ___ bigger.
If we ___ the rainforest, many creatures will lose their habitat.
items.why: first conditional: present simple after if

items.q: If I ___ the president, I would stop hunting.
items.why: unreal situation: past form after if

items.q: The crops will die ___ it rains soon.
If people recycled more, there ___ less rubbish.
What will happen to polar bears if the ice ___?
She ___ in the jungle if she wasn't afraid of insects.
Plants ___ grow if they don't get any light.
items.why: always true: present simple in both parts

items.q: If you ___ a tree tomorrow, I will help you.
If the population ___ (keep) growing, we will need more food.
If I had a big garden, I ___ (grow) my own vegetables.
Water always ___ (freeze) if the temperature drops below zero.
We ___ (not save) endangered animals unless we protect their habitat now.
If we ___ (not have) cars, the air in our city would be much cleaner.
items.why: would in the result, so past simple after if

items.q: What would you do if you ___ (see) someone dropping litter in the countryside?
items.why: would in the result, so past simple after if

items.q: If we will protect the environment, our children will thank us.
a: If we protect the environment, our children will thank us.

items.q: If I would live near the jungle, I would see monkeys every day.
a: If I lived near the jungle, I would see monkeys every day.
If I lived near the jungle, I'd see monkeys every day.

items.q: If you don't water a plant, it die.
a: If you don't water a plant, it dies.

items.q: at risk / will / if / be / many animals / continues / hunting
a: If hunting continues, many animals will be at risk.
Many animals will be at risk if hunting continues.

items.q: would / I / if / a lot of money / I / help / had / endangered animals
a: If I had a lot of money, I would help endangered animals.
I would help endangered animals if I had a lot of money.

units.title: Past perfect
notes: Form: had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had left. She hadn't eaten. Had they arrived?
Use it for an action that happened before another action or time in the past: When we got to the station, the train had gone.
The later action is in the past simple; the earlier one is in the past perfect: I was hungry because I hadn't had breakfast.
already, never, just and by the time are common with the past perfect.

items.q: When I got to the classroom, the lesson ___.
items.why: it started before I arrived: had + participle

items.q: She did badly in the exam because she ___ revised.
___ you studied French before you went to secondary school?
items.why: before another past action: Had + participle

items.q: By the time the school bus arrived, I ___ my breakfast.
items.why: by the time + past simple, then past perfect

items.q: I couldn't do my homework because I ___ my textbook at school.
After the head teacher had spoken, everyone ___ back to class.
items.why: the later action is past simple

items.q: He had never ___ a boarding school before that day.
The whiteboard was clean because someone ___ it.
When we ___ the timetable, we realised Monday was the hardest day.
I was nervous because I ___ (never attend) such a big school before.
When we arrived at the bus stop, the bus ___ (already leave). We had to walk.
The teacher was angry because nobody ___ (do) the homework.
By lunchtime I ___ (not eat) anything, so I was really hungry.
items.why: before a past time: hadn't + participle

items.q: ___ (the class start) by the time you got there?
We broke up for the holidays on Friday. By then we ___ (finish) all our exams.
She had wrote the essay before break time.
a: She had written the essay before break time.
items.why: the participle of write is written

items.q: When I arrived, the exam has already begun.
a: When I arrived, the exam had already begun.
items.why: before a past action use had, not has

items.q: He hadn't never failed an exam before.
a: He had never failed an exam before.
He hadn't ever failed an exam before.

items.q: had / my homework / I / realised / I / forgotten
a: I realised I had forgotten my homework.
items.why: past simple, then past perfect for the earlier action

items.q: the students / when / had / arrived / gone / the teacher / home
a: When the teacher arrived, the students had gone home.
The students had gone home when the teacher arrived.
When the students arrived, the teacher had gone home.
The teacher had gone home when the students arrived.
items.why: had + participle for the earlier action

units.title: Modals of obligation, necessity and advice: should, need to, have to, needn't
notes: should and shouldn't + infinitive give advice: You should pack a jumper.
need to + infinitive means it is important or necessary: You need to book early. It changes: she needs to, Do I need to?
have to + infinitive means it is necessary because of a rule or law: You have to wear a seat belt.
don't have to, don't need to and needn't (+ infinitive without to) mean it is not necessary: You needn't hurry.

items.q: You ___ check in online. It saves a lot of time.
Passengers ___ show their passports before they go on board. It's the law.
items.why: a law means it is necessary

items.q: You needn't ___ your own towels. The hotel has plenty.
We ___ to set off early to reach the port on time.
items.why: only need is followed by to here

items.q: The museum is free, so you ___ pay.
items.why: free means it is not necessary

items.q: He ___ need to unpack now. He can do it tomorrow.
You ___ leave your luggage alone at the airport. Someone might steal it.
___ we need to book the tour in advance?
items.why: questions with need to use do

items.q: My mum ___ renew her passport before we go away.
She ___ (not have to) get up early tomorrow because her flight is in the evening.
___ (I need to) bring my passport for a trip to Portugal?
Last summer we ___ (have to) wait five hours because our plane was held up.
items.why: the past of have to is had to

items.q: You ___ (should / needn't) hurry. The boat doesn't sail until six.
items.why: there is a lot of time, so not necessary

items.q: Tourists ___ (should / needn't) try the local food. It's delicious!
Yesterday my brother ___ (need to) buy a ticket on board because the office was closed.
You don't need pack a coat for this trip.
a: You don't need to pack a coat for this trip.
You needn't pack a coat for this trip.

items.q: Does he has to change trains in Madrid?
a: Does he have to change trains in Madrid?

items.q: You should arriving at the airport two hours early.
a: You should arrive at the airport two hours early.

items.q: to / early / we / need / set off / don't / tomorrow
a: We don't need to set off early tomorrow.
Tomorrow we don't need to set off early.

items.q: in / have / you / your seat belt / to / a car / wear
a: You have to wear your seat belt in a car.
In a car you have to wear your seat belt.

units.title: The passive: present, past and with modal verbs
notes: Passive is the verb be + past participle. Change be to show the tense.
Present simple passive: am, is, are + participle. These phones are made in Korea.
Past simple passive: was, were + participle. The bridge was built in 1890.
With modal verbs: modal + be + participle. Helmets must be worn. Use by for the person who does the action.

items.q: Thousands of photos ___ on this site every hour.
The video ___ down yesterday because it was rude.
Personal information must ___ private.
This song was shared ___ millions of fans.
items.why: by shows who did the action

items.q: ___ your account blocked last week?
items.why: singular subject in a past passive question

items.q: Comments can ___ by anyone who follows you.
The first text message ___ in 1992.
Rude comments ___ allowed on our school blog.
I ___ in a photo without my permission yesterday.
items.why: someone tagged me, so passive in the past

items.q: In general, new posts ___ (check) by a teacher before they appear.
items.why: present passive with a plural subject

items.q: The school's page ___ (create) in 2018.
Passwords should ___ (change) every few months.
We ___ (not tell) about the new rules until last Friday.
This app ___ (use) by more than a billion people every day.
The winners ___ (choose) by the judges last night.
items.why: the participle of choose is chosen

items.q: The photo was share by all my friends.
a: The photo was shared by all my friends.

items.q: These comments was written by a stranger.
a: These comments were written by a stranger.

items.q: Phones must be switch off in advance.
a: Phones must be switched off in advance.

items.q: be / in future / more carefully / photos / shared / should
a: Photos should be shared more carefully in future.
In future, photos should be shared more carefully.

items.q: was / by / the account / a hacker / blocked / last night
a: The account was blocked by a hacker last night.
Last night the account was blocked by a hacker.

units.title: Relative clauses: defining and non-defining
notes: Defining clauses say which person or thing we mean and have no commas: The boy who sits next to me is Italian.
who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession, where for places.
You can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was great.
Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas. Do not use that: My gran, who is eighty, still bakes.

items.q: The chef ___ restaurant won the prize is my uncle.
My grandma, ___ is eighty, still bakes bread every day.
items.why: between commas use who for people, not that

items.q: This is the pan ___ I use to fry eggs.
Valencia, ___ paella comes from, is on the coast.
The fish ___ we grilled last night was delicious.
This soup, ___ my dad made, tastes amazing.
items.why: between commas use which for things, not that

items.q: I have a friend ___ mum is a famous chef.
The cake ___ was really sweet.
items.why: that can be left out, but do not add it

items.q: People ___ don't eat meat can order the roast vegetables.
The woman ___ (who / which / whose) taught me to steam vegetables is Chinese.
My cousin, ___ (who / that / whose) restaurant is in Bilbao, works very hard.
The market ___ (which / where / who) we buy fresh fish opens at seven.
Gazpacho, ___ (that / which / who) is a cold soup, is perfect for summer.
items.why: non-defining clause about a thing: which

items.q: The knife ___ (who / which / whose) is on the table is very sharp.
Mr Ruiz, ___ (who / that / which) teaches us cooking, used to work in a hotel.
items.why: non-defining clause about a person: who

items.q: The pizza that we ordered it was cold.
a: The pizza that we ordered was cold.
The pizza which we ordered was cold.
The pizza we ordered was cold.
items.why: that replaces it, so do not repeat it

items.q: My brother, that is a chef, lives in London.
a: My brother, who is a chef, lives in London.
items.why: no that in a clause between commas

items.q: She's the woman which makes the best barbecue sauce.
a: She's the woman who makes the best barbecue sauce.
She's the woman that makes the best barbecue sauce.

items.q: I / the meal / was / yesterday / cooked / that / tasty
a: The meal that I cooked yesterday was tasty.

items.q: whose / have / cakes / I / a neighbour / are amazing
a: I have a neighbour whose cakes are amazing.

units.title: Articles: a/an, the and zero article
notes: a or an with a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time, and for jobs: I saw a fox. She's an engineer.
the when you mention something again, when there is only one, or when it is clear which one: The fox ran away. The moon is bright.
the with superlatives, seas, rivers, mountain ranges and plural country names: the best, the Atlantic, the Alps, the Netherlands.
No article for things in general, most countries and cities, meals, and by + transport: Life is short. We had lunch. I go by bus.

items.q: My aunt works as ___ engineer in the city.
items.why: a job, and engineer starts with a vowel sound

items.q: We visited some ruins. ___ ruins were two thousand years old.
___ wildlife needs clean rivers and forests.
They went sailing on ___ Mediterranean.
It's ___ most beautiful valley I have ever seen.
My cousin lives in ___ Netherlands.
We usually have ___ dinner at nine o'clock.
I go to the health centre by ___ bus.
Is there ___ health centre near your new flat?
items.why: first mention of any health centre

items.q: There is ___ (a / an / the) open space behind our building where we play football.
items.why: first mention, and open starts with a vowel sound

items.q: ___ (A / An / The) sun was very hot, so we stayed in.
I saw ___ (a / an / the) bug in my room last night. Then I couldn't sleep!
We went climbing in ___ (a / an / the) Pyrenees last season.
My mum is ___ (a / an / the) doctor at the local health centre.
Can you turn on ___ (a / an / the) air conditioning, please? It's boiling in here.
items.why: it is clear which one we mean

items.q: My father is architect.
The life in a big city can be stressful.
a: Life in a big city can be stressful.
items.why: no article for things in general

items.q: We moved to the France three years ago.
a: We moved to France three years ago.

items.q: in / is / the highest / Mount Everest / the world / mountain
a: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
The highest mountain in the world is Mount Everest.

items.q: my friend / an / lives in / old house / a / in / quiet valley
a: My friend lives in an old house in a quiet valley.
items.why: an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound

units.title: Reported speech
notes: After said or told, the tense usually moves back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, will to would, can to could.
Past simple and present perfect change to past perfect: 'I lost it.' He said he had lost it.
could, would, should and might do not change.
Pronouns and possessives change. say something (that); tell somebody (that): She told me that she liked her job.

items.q: 'I'm directing a musical,' she said. She said she ___ a musical.
items.why: am directing moves back to was directing

items.q: 'The film came out in May,' he said. He said the film ___ out in May.
items.why: past simple moves back to past perfect

items.q: He ___ us that the soundtrack was amazing.
'You should watch it,' said Ana. Ana said I ___ watch it.
'I have seen the recording,' said Leo. Leo said he ___ the recording.
items.why: present perfect moves back to past perfect

items.q: 'We will appear in the show,' they said. They said they ___ appear in the show.
The director explained ___ the role was very difficult.
'I love my role,' said the actor. The actor said he loved ___ role.
'I can't act,' said Tom. Tom said he ___ act.
'I work in a studio,' said the man. The man said he ___ (work) in a studio.
items.why: present simple moves back to past simple

items.q: 'We are recording a new song,' they said. They said they ___ (record) a new song.
items.why: are recording moves back to were recording

items.q: 'I forgot my lines,' said the actor. The actor said he ___ (forget) his lines.
items.why: past simple moves back to past perfect

items.q: 'The musical will be a success,' the director said. The director said the musical ___ (be) a success.
items.why: will be changes to would be

items.q: 'I have never directed a film,' she said. She said she ___ (never direct) a film.
items.why: present perfect moves back to past perfect

items.q: 'I might come to the performance,' said Dad. Dad said he ___ (might) come to the performance.
He told that the role was perfect for him.
a: He said that the role was perfect for him.
He told me that the role was perfect for him.
He told us that the role was perfect for him.
items.why: tell needs a person; say does not

items.q: She said she will buy the soundtrack.
a: She said she would buy the soundtrack.
items.why: will changes to would after said

items.q: They said they have finished the recording.
a: They said they had finished the recording.
items.why: have finished moves back to had finished

items.q: the film / that / she / had / said / already / seen / she
a: She said that she had already seen the film.

items.q: us / was / told / the performance / cancelled / the director
a: The director told us the performance was cancelled.

units.title: Reported questions
notes: Reported questions use statement word order and no question mark: 'Where is the bank?' He asked where the bank was.
Tenses move back as in reported statements: 'What are you doing?' She asked what I was doing.
do, does and did disappear: 'Where do you live?' She asked where I lived.
For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you ready?' She asked if I was ready.

items.q: She asked me where ___.
items.why: statement word order and no did

items.q: The teacher wondered ___ we had understood the joke.
'How old is your brother?' He asked how old ___.
items.why: subject before verb in reported questions

items.q: 'Can you swim?' They asked me if I ___ swim.
'Do you like jokes?' He asked if I ___ jokes.
items.why: do disappears and the verb moves back

items.q: 'Why are you complaining?' She asked why I ___.
items.why: are complaining moves back to was complaining

items.q: 'Will you remind me?' He asked if I ___ remind him.
'Have you promised to help?' Mum asked if I ___ promised to help.
items.why: have promised moves back to had promised

items.q: 'Where are your parents?' The police officer asked me where ___ parents were.
'Where do you work?' She asked me where I ___ (work).
items.why: do disappears; present moves back to past

items.q: 'Are you joking?' He asked if I ___ (joke).
items.why: are joking moves back to was joking

items.q: 'When will the bus arrive?' I asked when the bus ___ (arrive).
items.why: will arrive changes to would arrive

items.q: 'Did you warn them?' She asked if I ___ (warn) them.
items.why: past simple moves back to past perfect

items.q: 'Can you help me?' The tourist asked whether I ___ (can) help him.
'Why does she disagree?' He wondered why she ___ (disagree).
items.why: does disappears; present moves back to past

items.q: He asked me where was the station.
a: He asked me where the station was.
items.why: subject before verb in reported questions

items.q: They asked me why did I complain.
a: They asked me why I complained.
They asked me why I had complained.

items.q: He asked me that I was hungry.
a: He asked me if I was hungry.
He asked me whether I was hungry.
items.why: yes/no questions use if or whether, not that

items.q: asked / where / me / she / was / the library
a: She asked me where the library was.

items.q: if / wondered / I / would / he / come / the party / to
a: I wondered if he would come to the party.
He wondered if I would come to the party.

units.title: have something done
notes: Form: have + object + past participle. I have my eyes tested every year.
Use it when another person, usually a professional, does a job for you: We had the car repaired.
Compare: I cut my hair (I did it myself) and I had my hair cut (someone did it for me).
Change have to show the tense: she has, we had, I'm having, he is going to have, you should have.

items.q: We ___ our photo taken by a professional yesterday.
items.why: have + object + participle, in the past

items.q: She has her hair ___ every six weeks.
items.why: the participle of cut is cut

items.q: My parents are ___ the kitchen painted this week.
items.why: are + having for something in progress

items.q: He had ___ by a mechanic.
Where do you ___ your bike serviced?
items.why: after do use the infinitive have

items.q: We're going to have a new window ___ tomorrow.
My grandma ___ her shopping delivered every Friday.
Did you ___ your tooth taken out?
I didn't fix the laptop myself. I ___.
items.why: someone else did it: had + it + participle

items.q: My dad has his car ___ (wash) every Saturday.
She wants to have her ears ___ (pierce) for her birthday.
Last month we ___ (have) the roof repaired after the storm.
items.why: last month: past simple of have

items.q: You should have that strange noise in the car ___ (check).
I'm ___ (have) my bedroom painted at the moment, so I'm sleeping on the sofa.
He had his wallet ___ (steal) on the metro yesterday.
items.why: the participle of steal is stolen

items.q: I cut my hair at the hairdresser's yesterday.
a: I had my hair cut at the hairdresser's yesterday.
I got my hair cut at the hairdresser's yesterday.
items.why: the hairdresser did it, so have it cut

items.q: He had his suit make by a tailor.
a: He had his suit made by a tailor.

items.q: We had repaired the washing machine by a professional.
a: We had the washing machine repaired by a professional.
items.why: the object goes before the participle

items.q: every / has / tested / my mum / her eyes / year
a: My mum has her eyes tested every year.
Every year my mum has her eyes tested.

items.q: to / going / I'm / my phone / have / fixed / tomorrow
a: I'm going to have my phone fixed tomorrow.
Tomorrow I'm going to have my phone fixed.

units.title: Clauses of contrast, reason and purpose
notes: Contrast: although, whereas and while join two different or surprising ideas: Although it was cold, we swam. I love football, whereas my sister prefers tennis.
Do not use but in the same sentence as although.
Reason: because and as. We stayed in because it was raining. As it was late, we left.
Purpose: so that + subject + verb (often can, could, would); in order to + infinitive: I study hard so that I can pass.

items.q: ___ the job was stressful, she enjoyed it.
My brother manages a shop, ___ my sister works from home.
He updated the software ___ the computers would run faster.
items.why: purpose + subject + verb needs so that

items.q: She took a course in order ___ her skills.
We couldn't deliver the parcel ___ nobody was at home.
___ it was getting late, we decided to finish the meeting.
___ I like organising events, I don't enjoy dealing with complaints.
items.why: While can show contrast at the start

items.q: They hired more staff ___ produce more bikes.
items.why: purpose + infinitive needs in order to

items.q: He arrived on time ___ the traffic was terrible.
I saved my work every ten minutes ___ (so that / although) I wouldn't lose it.
___ (Although / Because) the task was difficult, she handled it really well.
He went to the office early in order ___ (to / that) install the new printers.
We cancelled the delivery ___ (because / whereas) the roads were flooded.
My dad calculates everything in his head, ___ (whereas / as) I always need a calculator.
She wrote the address down so that she ___ (would / will) not forget it.
items.why: after a past verb, so that + would

items.q: Although he was tired, but he finished the report.
a: Although he was tired, he finished the report.
He was tired, but he finished the report.
items.why: do not use although and but together

items.q: I called her for to arrange a meeting.
a: I called her to arrange a meeting.
I called her in order to arrange a meeting.
items.why: purpose is to + infinitive, not for to

items.q: We stayed inside because of it was raining.
a: We stayed inside because it was raining.

items.q: it was / we / although / the project / difficult / finished
a: Although it was difficult, we finished the project.
We finished the project although it was difficult.

items.q: so that / she / early / the meeting / could / left home / she / run
a: She left home early so that she could run the meeting.

units.title: Verbs with two objects
notes: Some verbs have two objects, a person and a thing: Dad gave me a watch.
Pattern 1: verb + person + thing, with no preposition: She sent her friend a postcard.
Pattern 2: verb + thing + to or for + person: She sent a postcard to her friend.
to with give, send, show, lend, tell, write, teach, offer, pass; for with buy, make, cook, choose, save, get.

items.q: My coach gave ___ some good advice.
items.why: verb + person + thing has no preposition

items.q: She sent a message ___ her whole team.
Dad bought a new racket ___ me.
Can you lend ___?
He showed his medal ___ everyone in the class.
My aunt made a costume ___ my little brother.
The teacher offered ___ a place in the school team.
items.why: verb + person + thing has no preposition

items.q: I told ___ the truth about my dream of being a pilot.
Grandpa read ___ a story every night.
items.why: verb + person + thing has no preposition

items.q: I wrote a long letter ___ (to / for) my favourite author.
Mum cooked a special dinner ___ (to / for) us after the match.
He taught the rules of chess ___ (to / for) his little sister.
We saved a seat ___ (to / for) you at the front.
She owes twenty euros ___ (to / for) her brother.
My friends chose a great present ___ (to / for) me.
He gave to his sister a book.
a: He gave his sister a book.
He gave a book to his sister.
items.why: no to when the person comes first

items.q: Can you lend your bike for me?
a: Can you lend your bike to me?
Can you lend me your bike?

items.q: She made a cake to her friend.
a: She made a cake for her friend.
She made her friend a cake.

items.q: sent / my cousin / me / from / a postcard / Italy
a: My cousin sent me a postcard from Italy.
My cousin from Italy sent me a postcard.

items.q: to / the coach / the trophy / the captain / gave
a: The coach gave the trophy to the captain.
The captain gave the trophy to the coach.
